clue.text: Designed for hat-eaters?

parts.note: people who swear they will eat their hat if proved wrong would want headgear named after an edible savoury pastry

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what kind of thing is made for people who eat hats.
explanation.walkthrough: A porkpie is a flat-crowned hat as well as a British cold meat pie, so it is the one hat a person who promised to 'eat my hat' could actually eat.
explanation.definitionFit: The pork pie hat is a style of felt headwear, while the pie is a pastry snack, giving edible headgear.

clue.text: "To-morrow to fresh woods and ---- new" (Milton)

parts.note: the missing word comes from the last line of Milton's elegy Lycidas, about grazing land

explanation.surface: The closing line of a pastoral poem, with one word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Lycidas ends 'To-morrow to fresh woods, and pastures new'; the blank on the page falls before 'new'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Milton's line the shepherd heads for new grazing meadows, fields where flocks feed.

clue.text: Pay back when about to take money

parts.note: re means about or concerning
tribute is money paid to a ruler or overlord

explanation.surface: Someone repays a debt when about to receive cash.
explanation.definitionFit: To retribute is to repay or give in return, an old verb behind retribution.

clue.text: Rained cats and dogs ?

parts.note: suggests a downpour, but read literally as showering animals, or showered with animal skins

explanation.surface: A remark on a very heavy downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: To pelt is to rain hard, and pelts are the skins of animals such as cats and dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: A pelting downpour is very heavy rain, the same idea as raining cats and dogs.

clue.text: Just the place for an outing

definitions.text: Just the place for an outing

parts.words: Just the place for an outing
parts.note: suggests a good spot for a trip, but means the place where people go out

explanation.surface: A recommendation of a good spot for a day trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outing' reads as a jaunt; take it literally as going out of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A way out of a building is the door people use for going out.

clue.text: Map with which to study the journey

parts.note: to con is an old word meaning to study or learn by heart
a tour is a journey round places

explanation.surface: A traveller asks for a map to study on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Map' works as a verb here: to contour land is to outline its shape on a chart.
explanation.definitionFit: A contour line on a chart traces the shape of the land, so contouring is a form of mapping.

clue.text: Father of Father Brown

parts.note: the priest-detective's creator, so his father in a literary sense

explanation.surface: A question about the parent of a priest named Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: G. K. Chesterton wrote the Father Brown detective stories, starting in 1910.
explanation.definitionFit: The English author G. K. Chesterton invented the priest-sleuth, making him the character's literary parent.

clue.text: Tips one the wink ?

parts.note: an idiom for giving someone a private signal, read literally as blinking at them

explanation.surface: Someone gives a friend a sly signal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip the wink' means give a secret hint; the answer is the formal verb for winking or blinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Nictitating is the technical word for blinking, so winking at someone is this action.

clue.text: Alternatively, cut down to the lowest deck

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
to lop is to cut off or prune

explanation.surface: An instruction to trim something right down to the bottom deck.
explanation.definitionFit: The orlop is the lowest deck of a sailing warship, below the waterline.

clue.text: But it doesn't mean you get your tax back

definitions.text: But it doesn't mean you get your tax back

parts.words: But it doesn't mean you get your tax back
parts.note: the form sent to the tax office has a name meaning to give back, though no money comes back

explanation.surface: A grumble about the tax form that never brings a refund.
explanation.walkthrough: A tax return is the form declaring income; the word also means getting something back, which it does not bring.
explanation.definitionFit: A tax return is the annual statement of income filed with the authorities.

clue.text: Small revolver ?

parts.note: read not as a pocket pistol but as a little body that circles round a larger one in orbit

explanation.surface: A request for a pocket-sized pistol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolver' suggests a gun; it means anything that revolves, here a moon circling a planet.
explanation.definitionFit: A moon is a body in orbit around a planet, revolving round it, and is small beside it.

clue.text: John's permitted to join the company

definitions.note: the definition is the man's name, with 's standing for 'is'

parts.note: CO is the usual abbreviation for company
let means allowed or permitted

explanation.surface: Someone named John is allowed to join a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: John Colet (1467-1519) was the Dean of St Paul's who founded St Paul's School in London; 'John's' reads as 'John is'.
explanation.definitionFit: John Colet was the Tudor scholar and churchman, so his surname completes the forename John.

clue.text: But they have their place in a league division

definitions.text: But they have their place in a league division

parts.words: But they have their place in a league division
parts.note: a league table is a division, yet some sides in it bear a name meaning joined together rather than divided

explanation.surface: A remark about teams finding a place in a football division.
explanation.walkthrough: Many British football clubs are called 'United' (Manchester United, Leeds United); the clue plays on teams named for unity sitting in a 'division'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clubs such as Manchester United are named for being joined together, the opposite of division.

clue.text: Robust type, addicted to the taws

definitions.meaning: the tawse is a leather strap once used to punish Scottish schoolchildren, so one fond of it is a user of the strap

explanation.surface: A hearty fellow who is all too keen on the punishment strap.
explanation.walkthrough: The taws (or tawse) is a Scottish schoolmaster's leather strap for beating pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: A strapping lad is a big sturdy one, and someone who keeps using the leather strap is one who straps.

clue.text: Musical tea-party

parts.note: an eighteenth-century word for a large afternoon tea party is also the name of an orchestral timpani

explanation.surface: An invitation to a tea party with music.
explanation.walkthrough: A kettledrum (timpani) is an orchestral drum, and in Georgian England the same word meant a large afternoon tea party.
explanation.definitionFit: The orchestral timpani is a musical instrument, and the old word also named a grand tea gathering.

clue.text: Birds that might inspire

parts.note: the name of these flightless Australian birds, rearranged, gives the nine goddesses of Greek myth who inspire poets and artists

explanation.surface: A thought about which birds could give a poet ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: Shuffle the birds' name and it spells MUSE, a source of inspiration; the clue hints at this without an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: These large flightless Australian ratites are birds, and their name holds the letters of the inspiring goddesses.

clue.text: Listen at ten, boy, and you'll be cheered!

parts.note: to hear is to listen
taken as the number ten written out
Ed is a boy's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: A command to tune in at ten o'clock and be cheered up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' is only a link here; any boy's name stands for a short name like ED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be heartened is to be given fresh courage and spirit, as cheering someone does.

clue.text: Rhymingly accompanied in the Floral Dance by the big bass drum

definitions.text: Rhymingly accompanied in the Floral Dance by the big bass drum

parts.words: Rhymingly accompanied in the Floral Dance by the big bass drum
parts.note: the song lists the band's instruments, and the word rhyming with drum is a brass one

explanation.surface: A recollection of the band in a famous Cornish song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Floral Dance' is a song about the Helston festival in Cornwall; its chorus runs 'big bass drum, bassoon, flute and euphonium', so the instrument rhymes with drum.
explanation.definitionFit: The euphonium is a tenor brass instrument named in the song's band beside the drum.

clue.text: They are certainly no match for one another

definitions.text: They are certainly no match for one another

parts.words: They are certainly no match for one another
parts.note: suggests rivals of unequal strength, but means things that do not form pairs

explanation.surface: A remark on two competitors of very unequal ability.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No match' reads as outclassed; take it as unmatched, like odd socks.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd items are ones that do not make a pair, unmatched like stray socks.

clue.text: Composer in a terrible rage after food

indicators.note: after places the mixed-up piece behind the food word

parts.note: a mess is a dish or portion of food

indicators.note: terrible means the letters of rage are thrown into a jumble

explanation.surface: A musician flies into a temper after a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' turns RAGE into AGER. André Messager (1853-1929) was a French composer and conductor.
explanation.definitionFit: André Messager was a French composer of operettas such as Véronique.

clue.text: Intrepid but confused about love can lead to Hell !

indicators.note: about means the mixed letters go around the other piece
confused tells us the letters of the word intrepid are mixed up

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: A warning that a bold but muddled lover is heading for damnation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges INTREPID to PERDITIN, and 'about' puts it round O.
explanation.definitionFit: Perdition is eternal damnation, the fate of souls condemned to the underworld.

clue.text: The recess provides some cheap sensationalism

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A complaint that an alcove is the setting for tabloid thrills.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a vaulted recess, usually at the east end of a church.

clue.text: One legislator has the skill to communicate

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
MP is a Member of Parliament, a lawmaker
art means skill, as in the art of persuasion

explanation.surface: A single lawmaker has a talent for getting a message across.
explanation.walkthrough: MP is a British Member of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart is to pass on information, which is to tell or convey it.

clue.text: A boxing bout? Thanks. But where?

definitions.note: the definition is a question word asking for a place, answered by a place name

parts.note: a spar is a practice bout in boxing
ta is British informal for thanks

explanation.surface: Someone offered a boxing match says thanks, but asks where it is.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is everyday British for 'thank you'. 'where?' points to a place: the ancient Greek city-state.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparta was a city-state of ancient Greece, so a place answering the question asking for a location.

clue.text: They contrived stage appearances of the gods

definitions.text: They contrived stage appearances of the gods

parts.words: They contrived stage appearances of the gods
parts.note: in Greek drama a crane lowered a god onto the stage, the deus ex machina, the god from the contraption

explanation.surface: A note on the devices behind divine entrances in theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase 'deus ex machina' means 'god from the machine': the crane that brought gods on stage in ancient theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatrical cranes and hoists are mechanical devices, the plural of the Latin machina in deus ex machina.

clue.text: It provides everything for tea

parts.note: both the porcelain service set out for tea and the country that grows tea leaves

explanation.surface: A claim about the one supplier of all that afternoon tea needs.
explanation.walkthrough: Porcelain tea services are called china, and the country China gave the world tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Porcelain cups, saucers and teapot make up the tea service, and the Asian country grows the leaf.

clue.text: Things stirring in the woods

parts.note: suggests creatures moving in a forest, but means kitchen utensils that stir and are often made of wood

explanation.surface: A hint of something moving about among the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the woods' suggests a forest; read it as wooden utensils used for stirring, or courting couples cuddling there.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooden cooking utensils with a bowl at one end are used for stirring pots.

clue.text: Homer's dialect

parts.note: the mixed literary Greek of the Iliad and Odyssey is named after the heroic poetry it was used for

explanation.surface: A question about the language of the Greek poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Scholars call Homer's literary Greek the Epic dialect, after the genre of long heroic poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Homeric Greek is the language of heroic narrative poetry, the kind of verse the Iliad is.

clue.text: A party has one excuse

parts.note: Lib is short for Liberal, a political party
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A political party has a single excuse ready.
explanation.walkthrough: LIB stands for the Liberal Party, then a major British party.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a plea of having been elsewhere, so a reason offered to clear oneself.

clue.text: Bringing news of again turning left ?

parts.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
porting a ship's helm turns it to port, the left side

explanation.surface: A question about news of someone turning left once more.
explanation.walkthrough: Port is the left-hand side of a ship, so porting is turning to the left.
explanation.definitionFit: A journalist covering a story is giving an account of it, which is bringing news.

clue.text: Most ran in a tizzy to the crossbeam

indicators.note: in a tizzy means flustered, so the letters of most ran are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Most people rushed in a panic towards the beam.
explanation.definitionFit: A transom is a horizontal bar across a window or above a door, a beam set crosswise.

clue.text: Here's to the. ---- whose dimples we prize" (Sheridan)

definitions.text: Here's to the. ---- whose dimples we prize" (Sheridan)

parts.words: Here's to the. ---- whose dimples we prize" (Sheridan)
parts.note: the missing word is from the drinking song in Sheridan's School for Scandal, toasting a delightful woman

explanation.surface: A line from a toast in a Restoration-style comedy, with one word blank.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'Here's to the maiden of bashful fifteen' comes from Sheridan's 1777 play The School for Scandal; a later verse toasts a dimpled enchantress.
explanation.definitionFit: The song toasts a delightful, captivating woman whose dimples win admirers.
